doc.title: Lorraine Feather interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 22, 2023

title: Dick Hyman and the stride album
summary: Fats Waller's 'Turn on the Heat' leads her to write 'Cezanne' and Hyman urges her to do a whole stride album.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: All right. I’ll keep my eye out for some funding for that. Let me run a couple names by you that I believe you’ve worked with. Dick Hyman?

Oh. Well Dick Hyman was my parents’ friend when we were back in New York. I knew him a little bit, Dick and Julia. But when I was living in northern California and my dad had passed away and I was going through a lot of CDs and re-issues in the garage to help my mom decide what to donate. And I came across this Fats Waller double CD called “Turn on the Heat.” And I just absolutely fell in love with it. My parents hadn’t played much stride music because it was too old fashioned for them. But I just loved it. I used to drive around in my Volkswagen Beetle with a CD changer, listen to it over and over and over again. And I was writing at this time lyrics for cartoons. But I wasn’t employed at the time and I thought I want to do something kind of challenging and fun. So I wrote lyrics to something called “Smashing Thirds” and titled it “Cezanne,” — or actually it had a different title at the time, it was called “No for an Answer” because it was about how everyone gave the painter Cezanne, they all told him no until he was, you know, pretty much dead. And I sent it to Dick Hyman because he is the stride guy and I thought he might get a kick out of it. I put some live musicians around it and I used the Fats

Waller sample. So Dick Hyman calls me up, and mind you I really didn’t know him at all except just vaguely. And he said, “All right,” he said, “you have to do a whole album of these stride piano pieces with your lyrics because who else is going to do it? And I like it because,” he said, “it’s like Lambert, Hendricks & Ross only the music is much older, even much older” he said, and I’ll plan it. But I don’t have time right now so find somebody else and then when it’s time” — and he began sending me all of these stride pieces, and I just kept going. And about two weeks after this my mom passed away and Dick called again and he said, “You need something to do right now, just keep working on the album.” So I worked with Mike Lang, who sadly, I mean Dick Hyman at 96 still sounded great when I talked to him a few weeks ago. Mike Lang, the pianist in L.A. who was helping me on some of this has sadly died. But he kind of got me started and then I went to Florida and finished up with Dick. And we did a few gigs together. But it was just incredible because he just kind of told me to do it. And I thought it would be fun so I did it.
He’s something else. He’s capable of just about anything I guess.
And he’s so modest. He’s funny and dignified and wry and just one of the most admirable people I’ve ever met.
